title: Transcribe Names from Silver Trophies: A Review Guide
description: Recover winner names from silver trophy photographs, check difficult letters and initials, use supporting evidence and preserve uncertainty in your club archive.
html:
Transcribing a silver trophy means recording what the inscription supports, not merely producing a plausible list of names. Reflections and wear can turn a clear-looking photograph into uncertain evidence. A careful workflow separates taking the image, reading the letters and deciding what the historical record should say.

1. Establish the trophy and its date range

Record the competition name and the earliest and latest visible years. Photograph the whole trophy before the close-ups. Check whether winners are engraved on the bowl, on bands around a base or on individual plates. Missing one area can create an apparent gap that is simply a gap in the photographs.

2. Make a difficult inscription visible

Use soft light and compare several camera angles. If the surface reflects a bright window or flash over the lettering, move the camera or light and retake the image. For a curved band, capture overlapping sections rather than relying on the compressed text at the edge of one picture.

Keep the physical object safe and do not alter a historic surface to improve a photograph. The trophy photography checklist explains how to check the image set before returning the trophy to the cabinet.

3. Treat the first reading as a proposal

Trophy Guru uses the source photographs to propose winner names and years. Review those readings against the images. AI can misinterpret an initial, a date or an unfamiliar surname, and the fact that a proposed name looks familiar is not enough to confirm it.

Do not claim that software can detect microscopic details or reconstruct lettering which is absent from the photograph. If the source is unreadable, another photograph or another historical source is needed. Some records may remain unresolved.

4. Separate the letters from the person’s identity

Suppose a fictional inscription clearly reads “J. Brown”. The transcription supports those characters. Expanding that to “James Brown” is a separate claim which requires evidence. A current membership directory may not cover the historical period, and two members may share the same initials.

Check contemporary result sheets, an honours book, minutes or another relevant source. In the club’s research notes, record which source supported the decision. This gives a future reviewer something stronger than a confident guess.

5. Resolve dates and gaps carefully

Compare each digit of the year, especially around scratches or worn strokes. Check the relationship between the date and the correct name. Where several names are engraved closely together, the layout may matter as much as the individual characters.

An absent year can have several explanations. A plate may be missing, a photograph may omit a section or a competition may not have been held. Do not choose an explanation without supporting evidence. Add a missing winner manually only when a reliable club source supports the entry.

6. Confirm, export and share

Once the club is satisfied with the evidence, confirm the reviewed records. Export a CSV copy and retain the original photographs separately. Decide which information is ready for publication and who will maintain it when the next competition is completed.

An electronic honours board lets members explore the confirmed history by year, trophy and person. Our public demonstration uses fictional records to show that experience; it is not evidence of a transcription accuracy rate.

You can try your first trophy free, with up to 12 saved photographs and no payment card required. Use that pilot to judge the workflow on your own silverware before estimating the rest of the collection.
